text: Mr Radzi and Ms Risa show us how strong foundations enable families to thrive.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Puan Jumaini demonstrates how dedication to preserving heritage becomes a valuable contribution to future generations.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Mr Muhammad Nor Hafiz exemplifies how entrepreneurial spirit, when supported by the community, transforms aspirations into success and opportunity.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Puan Latipah's journey from participant to volunteer coordinator embodies the meaningful cycle of receiving support and giving back that strengthens our community.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: These individuals illustrate the essence of a "we first" society, where personal development contributes to collective progress and where every act of service creates positive impact throughout our community.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This is the spirit we hope to see everyone in our community embody.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We have much to look forward to in our collective future.

speaker: The Acting Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Let us do so by moving forward together, with one heart.

text: Having shared with us the developments of your engagement with students in Middle East, could you also give us an update as to some early plans the Government may be making with regard to planning ahead of the Haj season?

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: I shared about how we are continuously engaging our students in the Middle East.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: In fact, I had a very good session with them last night, more than an hour.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: No doubt, they are very concerned, but they asked mainly for advice on what they should do and the various scenarios.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: And we just also heard Minister of State Gan Siow Huang's message earlier.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The message that I shared with them was to continue to be connected and also, look after one another.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: This is something that they have been getting.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: MUIS have been working very closely with them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Quite a number of them also experienced incidents in June.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: For the seniors, they are able to handle and manage this better than the juniors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: So, you see a different type of steps being taken by the different countries: some are doing it online; others still have face-to-face classes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: One thing that I also shared with them is to also keep in touch with their families.

text: As expected, many of the family members are very concerned.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: For Umrah, as I shared, we are in touch with AMTAS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: AMTAS released an advisory where it concurred with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs' (MFA's) advisory.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: For those who are already in Saudi Arabia, I urge them to register with MFA so that they can receive timely updates, as the situation develops.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: And for others who wish to make changes to their travel plans, I would like to thank AMTAS who have been reaching out to the travel agents to exercise understanding and to see how we can help travellers to review, postpone, or make travel arrangements for affected travel plans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: So, we will closely monitor the latest developments.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: Chairman, I thank the Acting Minister for sharing about the revamped Malay Heritage Centre, as well as setting up the research unit.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: In some ways, we are looking back towards wanting to preserve the heritage and traditions of the Malay community.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi
text: But I wonder whether there are initiatives to be able to celebrate and also share and showcase our unique Malay identity towards others, so that we can celebrate the diversity that we have here in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: You can see the expanded role of the Malay Heritage Centre goes beyond just cultural preservation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: It will showcase how Singaporean Malay identity has evolved into something truly distinctive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: It comes along with a deeply rooted Malay identity and traditions perspective, but we have to recognise that our identity is uniquely and precisely being shaped by our multicultural environment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: And this is where you see many Malays have excelled across many sectors and they come forward to contribute, regardless of race, language or religion, and all these are also being done while deeply rooted to our culture and faith.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: So, this balance is what sets our Singaporean Malays apart from the rest.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: And if you look at the Intangible Cultural Heritage Mentorship programme, it will help us to continue this journey.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We have built this process of building our community and nation over the years, where you can see certain values in the Malay community that exemplify Singapore as a whole as well, in terms of its self-determination, openness and resilience.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The research unit will look at various aspects of this journey as well, but looking at, in terms of the heritage tradition, the arts and culture and cultural history and Nusantara.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Some of these will present opportunities for our people, including non-Malays, to come on board this journey and share the joy of our nation building.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: So, it is something exciting, something that we have built together.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: My hope is that anyone who visits Malay Heritage Centre or takes part in the programme will know that this is a distinctively unique Singaporean Malay identity that has progressed and something that we should be proud of.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Chairman, can I ask my first clarification in Malay? :   Mr Chairman, caring for our elderly is not just about programmes – it is about strengthening values like respect, responsibility and compassion in our families and communities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: As shared, the programme is spearheaded by Minister of State Rahayu "Langkah Digital" is another area where it gives us another opportunity to expand our outreach in a way that can help the community.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: I think in the way we develop our community, we have to bring in as much resources as there are out there.

text: Especially those who have done well, to come back, give back, and mentor and nurture and provide the impetus for each and every one of our children, even those who are still working, to have that aspiration to develop further.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: On the first point. :   On the first point, the Santunan Emas programme is a ground-up programme that is also holistic.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: But what is interesting about this programme is how it collaborates with organisations or agencies, like Agency for Integrated Care and NHG Health.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: When I heard about this programme, I received feedback that it is very engaging and sparked the interest of our seniors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: They told me they want to hear religious sermons or words of encouragement from Ustaz Fatris, and I can see this is something very appealing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: I am very grateful to everyone who started this programme, because they started small, not knowing its potential, but we can see that it is able to generate interest as well as provide development opportunities for the seniors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, when we speak about social cohesion today, the deeper question is not just how well we get along, but how confident Singaporeans feel about who we are becoming.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Externally, the world is becoming more uncertain, contested and polarised.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Internally, Singaporeans, especially younger Singaporeans, are thinking more actively about identity, voice, fairness and belonging.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Together, these shifts mean that social cohesion today is no longer just about co-existence, but about whether people feel anchored in a shared sense of who we are.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It recognises that Singapore has always been open and evolving, and that with a strong sense of self, we can remain open without insecurity.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: But if multiculturalism is our anchor, then the key question is how Singaporeans experience and live that anchor in everyday terms.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: What does it mean today to be a Singaporean Chinese, a Singaporean Malay, a Singaporean Indian, Eurasian – not as fixed categories from the past, but as identities shaped by shared experiences, common values and participation in modern Singapore?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: How do our arts, sports, heritage spaces and youth platforms help people internalise this rather than just leaving identity to be shaped implicitly by fragmented or external narratives?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: When identity is under-articulated or not felt, it creates space for pessimism and quiet social distancing even if surface harmony remains.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: As such, beyond delivering strong individual initiatives, how is the Ministry intentionally shaping a coherent narrative of what defines us as Singaporeans today, one that builds confidence in our multicultural identity and a shared sense of belonging, especially amongst younger Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: And how does the Ministry assess whether its work is strengthening this deep foundational long-term social cohesion?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Trials can be highly competitive and places are of course limited.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: As a result, some students who simply wish to try something new or participate recreationally find themselves excluded from school sports altogether.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: This risks narrowing participation to those who are already skilled when the developmental nature of sport lies precisely in allowing more young people to experience it.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Such pathways could allow students to discover interest and develop confidence before deciding whether they wish to pursue a sport more seriously.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Sports also provide one of the most natural spaces for young Singaporeans of different abilities and backgrounds to interact.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: When students train and play together, they learn cooperation, perseverance and mutual respect.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: In building a "we first" society, such shared experiences matter.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: School sports should remain both a pathway for excellence and a platform for broad participation.

text: I would therefore appreciate if the Minister could share how policy can better balance these objectives while ensuring that student well-being and academic balance are safeguarded.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Chairman, sports and outdoor education play a formative role in shaping the resilience, confidence and sense of belonging for our youths.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I have previously declared that I was in the national youth bowling team.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: But beyond that chapter, my journey in sports began simply playing basketball at the community centre with my father and at school during recess with friends.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It progressed to competing in bowling, javelin and shot put in school and having my Alex Honnold moments on the rock climbing walls as a young adult when I started working.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: What stayed with me was not achievement or the medals, but the lessons in discipline, teamwork and perseverance.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: For many youths, sport provides a constructive third space where they build identity, friendships and resilience.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Studies have also found that youths who participate regularly in sports report significantly higher life satisfaction and lower stress levels than their less active peers.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In this House, we often focus on the Olympics, major games and elite performance.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: These are important and we should continue supporting high-performance athletes.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: But if our focus is too narrow, we risk overlooking the broader base where many youths are meaningfully engaged.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: My sense is that the number of athletes represented by National Sport Associations (NSAs) which do not qualify for the Olympics greatly outnumber those in the few sports we often highlight.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Many sports, such as tchoukball, rollersports, dragonboat and others, are sustained by passionate communities, many of whom are youths.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: These platforms may not carry Olympic status, but they play an important developmental role.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Could the Government play a bigger role in facilitating greater after-hours access to facilities such as schools as training grounds?

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: If we truly believe sport is for youth development, then breadth of opportunity must matter as much as podium outcomes.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: If sports shape youths in familiar community spaces, outdoor education shapes them in unfamiliar terrain.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I am a grateful beneficiary of the Outward Bound School (OBS), having attended the five-day OBS course in Secondary 3 and later returning for longer programmes on the Ubin Campus and the final one in the mountains of Korea.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: But as this expansion progresses, may I ask, what is the next milestone for OBS Singapore?

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: As we strengthen local access, could we also consider extending more overseas OBS experiences in a calibrated way?

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Exposure to different terrains and cultures stretches youths in ways sometimes our domestic environments cannot.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: While OBS remains a national cornerstone, continued support for other outdoor education providers, working with parties like the Outdoor Adventure Education Council, would strengthen the broader ecosystem and widen access for youths with different interests and needs.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Mr Chairman, I am sure every Member of this House is aware of the issues arising from the increasing popularity of pickleball in our neighbourhoods.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: I received some very angry complaints from both players and residents right after I became a Member of Parliament.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: It is, let us face it, a noisy game.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: But the tensions are not limited to our Housing and Development Board (HDB) neighbourhoods too.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: I have had complaints about pickleball noise from the grounds of a private club.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: For my ward, I have been pushing for what I call an 80% solution.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: She is a very considerate neighbour and had started using them because they reduce noise levels considerably.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: But it is only an 80% solution because it is, of course, impossible to please everyone.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Some players resisted the foam balls because they felt different and were not competition ready.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: They were happy to take the free foam balls, they just will not use them.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Which is ironic, because our neighbourhood courts are not competition-compliant either.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Some residents, on the other hand, feel that this does not go far enough and would prefer pickleball to be banned entirely.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: In political science, there is the concept of positive and negative rights.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Our pickle over pickleball can be a classic case study of the tensions between both.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The right to play clashing with the right to peace and quiet.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Political scientists will tell you that this is a zero-sum game.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: In a dense city like ours, neither right can be absolute.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: We must approach it from a framework of compromise and give-and-take.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: That is the only way to preserve harmony in our society.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Participation in community sports is growing and demand for neighbourhood and precinct level facilities is rising.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: We should welcome this, but yet, as we have seen, it can also easily become a source of discord, instead of bonding in our communities.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: So, this cannot be just about trying to meet the demand.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: It would be very easy to turn many under-utilised spaces in our neighbourhoods into more pickleball courts, or other sports courts for that matter.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: But the most convenient place may not be the best place, or even the right place.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Would noise and human traffic be an issue?

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Would it disturb the residents in the neighbourhood?

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Can the noise be contained at the location chosen?

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: We should learn the lessons and we can preamp much of these tensions.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The last thing that we want to do is to create more tensions and unhappiness in our communities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is likely to become even more popular.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While many enjoy the physical and social benefits of play, complaints abound.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Some grouse about limited availability of shared courts, while others object to the noise.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In response to the hundreds of noise complaints received, some Town Councils have chosen to restrict playing time or to ban play altogether.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yet as many have faced intense lobbying efforts for expanded hours.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There is generally sufficient space for the game and the ceiling will limit upward noise transmission.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To further contain noise, retractable sound curtains can be easily installed along the parameter.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There is some precedence for conversion of existing infrastructure into pickleball courts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One objection is that there is an opportunity cost to forgone income, since such lots may generate potential revenue.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This has sometimes been the Ministry of National Development's (MND's) response to requests for converting carpark spaces to other uses, such as community gardens.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But in many newer estates, including Sengkang, these lots are already underutilised, and almost always empty.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The opportunity cost of forgone income is entirely imaginary.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, even if guest parking needs are elevated in certain periods – such as during holidays, where visitations are more common – swing barricades can easily be installed and opened to allow access on such occasions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Another objection to safety, is that safety might be compromised when carparks are used beyond their designated purpose.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, when Sengkang Town Council proposed this idea to MND, the response begged the question: "The playing of pickleball and any other recreational activities are not an approved use of the HDB carpark currently as HDB multi-storey car parks were designed and built primarily for parking only." But multi-storey car parks are already used for other functions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Temporary office space, such as HDB site offices, is sometimes located at the upper floors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There is also the Courier Hub Scheme that is applicable in select multi-storey car parks.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: A third objection is that regulation pickleball courts often call for a five-metre height minimum.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But there are multi-storey car parks, including those in Sengkang, that fulfill this requirement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Let us get this done, for the sake of players and non-players – and perhaps, long-suffering MPs.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Chairman, to go for a run, all you need is a pair of shoes.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is no membership, no queue, no need to travel to a gym.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Strength training has no equivalent and I want to make the case today that it should.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Strength training is not just for the muscle bound body builder, it is for everyone.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Bone density peaks around age 30 and decline steadily thereafter.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Aerobic exercise slows the decline, but strength training has the potential to reverse it.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Building bone, building muscle and reducing the risk of falls and fractures in ways that cardio alone cannot.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Before my daughter was born six months ago, I went to the gym two or three times a week.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Since she arrived, I have gone fewer than 10 times in total, not because I do not want to go, but because 15 minutes travelling there and then 15 minutes back, is 30 minutes that a young father cannot find.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If there were a resistance station at my void deck, I would use it every other day, I am sure of this.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The elderly resident maintaining muscle and bone density, the beginner who would not know where to start in a commercial gym, the time press parent.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The barrier looks different for each, but it is the same barrier.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They are affordable, well distributed, well equipped, but they require a trip.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: You need to check if the capacity is full and often, at peak hours, you need to queue for equipment.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many already include strength oriented equipment, but effective strength training requires progressive overload, the ability to increase resistance as you get stronger.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The beginner starts at five kilogrammes and then moves up to 20, 30, 40 over time.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Instead, they largely feature equipment that focuses on encouraging mobility and fixed resistance machines.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In their current guide, they serve a limited demographic.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should increase their utility and therefore, I have three suggestions for the Ministry.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: You can upgrade these first, and for upcoming plan builds, incorporate variable resistance equipment from day one.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Two, we should work with NParks to incorporate variable resistance equipment into park fitness corners as they come up for renewal or upgrading.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And lastly, for HDB fitness corners under town council management, we should develop a national framework with pre-qualified standards, recommended suppliers and co-funding pathways through Sports SG, so Town Councils can upgrade without running full procurement exercises.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: The Ministry also alluded to the eventual consolidation of the HPSI and the Singapore Sports School.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: For many years, Singapore's sports landscape has involved multiple institutions working across different stages of the athlete's journey, from youth identification to elite performance.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: The intent behind this consolidation is therefore an important one: to create a more integrated system that supports athletes more effectively throughout their development.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Could the Minister provide an update on the progress of this consolidation?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: In particular, how will the new structure strengthen athlete development pathways, ensure smoother transitions from youth potential to elite performance?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: How will the system better coordinate coaching, sports science and athlete management so that promising young athletes receive consistent support as they progress?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: At the same time, I seek to ask how the Ministry will ensure that sporting excellence is balanced with education and well-being, because many of our young athletes must juggle training commitments with academic responsibilities?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: How will MCCY and SportSG ensure that this integration reduces fragmentation across agencies and ultimately leads to stronger long-term outcomes for Team Singapore?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: I would therefore appreciate the Minister's update on how this new structure is taking shape.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Chairman, I declare my interest as a Vice-President of an NSA.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Sports play an important role in national identity, community health and youth development.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Singapore has enjoyed notable successes on the international stage and grassroots sport participation has grown.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: But if we look more closely at the institutional backbone of our sporting ecosystem, the NSAs, there are structural pressures that deserve attention.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Recent public reporting has shown that private sponsorship for sports remain limited.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Many NSAs and athletes have acknowledged the difficulty of securing sustained corporate backing.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: This means that associations remain heavily reliant on Government subventions and short-term grants.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Whilst NSAs are mainly run by volunteers, MCCY shared in Parliament that Sport Singapore and the Singapore National Olympic Council are working to strengthen their governance and operational capabilities.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: But it also underscores the reality that many associations operate with lean secretariats and limited professional depth.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Furthermore, SportSG funding is tied to governance and strategic planning requirements.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: While this promotes accountability, it also means that associations with weaker institution capacity may struggle to secure stable, multi-year support, reinforcing a cycle of fragility.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Against this backdrop, feedback from athletes and NSA leaders continues to highlight structural constraints: difficulty retaining coaching talent due to funding uncertainty; challenges in building robust athlete development pathways beyond the elite tier; limited resources for sports science; injury prevention and sustained grassroots outreach.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: If sport is to remain a pillar of national well-being and identity, then our NSAs must be equipped not only with passion, but with stability, professionalism and long-term resilience.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: In this changed, turbulent world, we must invest just as deliberately in the arts, sport and the cultural ecosystems because these are the human and societal foundations that shape who we are as Singaporeans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: In an AI-led world, creative work, sport and cultures will not disappear.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: They will become even more valuable as distinctly human pursuits.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Allow me to make four points in my cut.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: First, on the sustainability of our arts and sports practitioners.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: In both sectors, talent alone is not enough for excellence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Career spans can be short, income streams uneven, with the burden of support often falling on their families.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: In the arts, many operate as freelancers or pursue portfolio careers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: But to sustain their work at a high level, practitioners must be equipped as professionals able to protect and sustain their work.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: But could the Ministry consider further strengthening these efforts with more structured support for career transitions?

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: This could include providing modules in areas such as sponsorship management, personal brand development and entrepreneurship so that our national athletes are better equipped to support themselves beyond their competitive years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Financial viability also matters in heritage cultural enterprises.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: As long-standing businesses close, could MCCY consider establishing a targeted succession support initiative, providing advisory support, mentorship and transition planning to help heritage cultural enterprises pass sustainably to the next generation?

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Let us ensure that rising cost of living does not hinder Singaporeans from pursuing their talents in these domains.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Second, on the participation in the arts and sports.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: A vibrant arts and sporting culture also depends on broad participation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: A broad base helps to strengthen the talent pipeline.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: I am encouraged by arts programmes in community spaces and the showcasing of our national athletes in our neighbourhoods.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: These initiatives embed culture and sport in everyday life.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: I would welcome updates by the Ministry on utilisation – whether it is reaching new audiences and increasing regular engagement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Similarly, could the Ministry consider piloting a participation-based mechanism such as an SG Sport Pass, where funding is directed specifically towards programmes delivered by accredited coaches?

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Not only will this broaden access to structured sports participation, it will also incentivise coach certification and upscaling and strengthen the likelihood of our coaches, many of whom operate as small businesses and enterprises.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: My third point is on enhancing ecosystem financing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: But we can do more to crowd in and catalyse sustained giving in the arts and sports by corporations and private donors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: To do so, can the Government consider extending enhanced tax deductions of up to 400% tied to long-term support for these sectors, given their importance to national resilience and unity?

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: A structure that supports multi-year giving pledges with higher deductions will provide planning certainty for arts groups and our sporting organisations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: If we are prepared to incentivise investments in technological capability because it strengthens economic competitiveness, we should also be deliberate in incentivising cultural investments that strengthen cohesion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: My fourth point is on projecting our national identity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: The arts and sport do more than bring us together at home.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: They also project who we are in the world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Just as our athletes proudly fly the Singapore flat at major international games, could MCCY consider developing a strategy for high-potential arts and cultural groups to perform on the world's most prominent stages and international festivals?

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: When our artists and creators showcase their work on these international platforms, it helps to project confidence in who we are as a nation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: If we are proud and confident of our identity, we should also present that identity to the world with equal confidence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, as we build a future-ready economy, we must also build a future-ready society, one that can help us thrive in these uncertain times.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: The returns may not always appear in economic numbers, but they will be reflected in our pride that we share as a nation.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As the Government now moves forward to develop the site into a public space, it is important that the process takes into account national heritage needs, exercises sensitivity and respect for the dignity of the site, and also to take into account the concerns and needs of neighbouring residents at every stage of the planning process.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: After all, for neighbours, they will be the most greatly impacted by this development.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The historic significance of 38 Oxley Road is beyond dispute.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It was here that our founding leaders held the consequential discussions that led to our governance.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: On the other hand, let us be mindful that 38 Oxley Road does not exist in isolation.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It sits within a quiet, established residential enclave.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The daily lives of residents in the vicinity will be directly affected by the transformation of 38 Oxley Road from a private residence into a public heritage space.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Since the Government announced its intention to gazette the site, residents have come forward to share their concerns with me.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Multiple residents have expressed worry that the conversion of the site into a public space could bring significantly more vehicles, tour buses and pedestrians into an area that, as one resident put it, "isn't built for that purpose".

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Residents have highlighted the longstanding problem of non-residents using their private car parks, given the absence of gantries or security at their entrances.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If the site attracts large numbers of visitors, where will they park?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Third, the impact of human traffic – noise, crowds and the disruption to the tranquil character of the estate.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Residents recalled the surge of visitors in 2017 during the public dispute over the site's future and fear a repeat on a far larger and more permanent scale.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They understand and can agree that it is important for visitors, including our future generations, to visit and understand the significance of this site, but they also worry that the place will lose its sense of dignity.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They are practical everyday realities and they deserve to be treated with the seriousness they merit.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: MCCY, as the lead Ministry responsible for the preservation and development of the site, will need to plan and coordinate with the relevant Ministries and agencies very carefully.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Ministry of Transport must be engaged on traffic management, parking solutions and public transport access.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Proposals such as designating alternative access points, creating drop-off zones for tour coaches and improving pedestrian infrastructure along Oxley Road should be seriously studied.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Ministry of National Development must address building and estate maintenance issues.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Residents have expressed hope that the gazetting will bring upgrades to the surrounding estate, including improvements to walkways and infrastructure.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There is also the question of whether planning controls and height restrictions in the area may be adjusted, which will affect residents' property rights and interests.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Ministry of Trade and Industry must work to minimise disamenities caused by tourism.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If the site were to be developed into a heritage park, there must be careful management of visitor flows, operating hours and commercial activity to ensure that the residential character of the neighbourhood is preserved.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Property consultants have noted that planners will need to facilitate adequate car and coach parking and drop-off zones.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The most important point I wish to make is this – residents must not be informed of decisions only after they are made.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They must be involved in shaping those decisions from the very beginning.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These should not be just one-off feedback sessions, but an ongoing dialogue throughout the planning, design, construction and operational phases of the development.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The preservation of 38 Oxley Road as a national monument is a significant step in safeguarding Singapore's founding history for future generations.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But a monument that is developed in a neighbourhood, without mitigation measures, risks becoming a source of division rather than unity.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Let us build this heritage space the Singapore way – through careful planning, inter-agency coordination and, most importantly, through genuine partnership with the residents whose lives will be most directly affected.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Chairman, Tanjong Pagar-Tiong Bahru is a place where many of Singapore's stories began.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our very first Community Centre in Tiong Bahru, one of our first Residents' Committees in Tanjong Pagar Plaza, our beloved Tiong Bahru Market set amidst a beautiful pre-war public housing estate and, over at Tanjong Pagar, shophouses filled with clan associations juxtaposed against one of our very first mixed-use public housing developments, Tanjong Pagar Plaza, juxtaposed against the towering 55-floor The Pinnacle ＠ Duxton – until it is overtaken by the 60-floor Pearl's Hill Build-To-Order (BTO) coming up soon.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They contain stories of our residents who have stayed here for many decades and they are living repositories of memory, culture and identity.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, heritage by itself does not sustain itself.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If it is to be meaningful, it needs to be refreshed and shared with each new generation.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Today, our neighbourhood is home to many new families, young residents and international communities who may not know the stories of the earlier generation staying here.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And it has been my mission to refresh our legacies and connect our generations in Tanjong Pagar-Tiong Bahru.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Where heritage is lived and shared, it will become a bridge between the past and the present and the future generations – and together, we will achieve my vision for Tanjong Pagar, Tiong Bahru, to be a living community where every generation finds its place in the Singapore story.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: At home, our super-ageing population, complex social needs and weakening social ties strain both the social and health sectors.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In my Budget speech, I spoke about community networks protecting against isolation.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In Bishan, mothers gather at playgrounds, taking turns to host playdates and support one another.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: At Bishan Community Club, a group of young widows called HopeHerd ensures no widow journeys alone.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Like elephants, they form a herd so mothers and children can grieve and heal together.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Rotaract Club of Raffles City runs community projects and has launched cross-border collaborations with their twin club in Kuala Lumpur, including the inaugural Rotaract ASEAN Young Leaders' Exchange.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These ground-up efforts show that our communities already possess deep social capital.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When trusted and supported, residents take ownership, supporting families, combating isolation, strengthening mental well-being.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What would supercharge them is sustained, low-barrier funding.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Japan's Fureai Kippu lets volunteers earn credits caring for the elderly.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Switzerland's St Gallen Zeitvorsorge, backed by their Federal Social Insurance Office, records volunteer hours in social security accounts for future use.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Time-banking gives dignity because no one is a passive beneficiary; everyone contributes.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Skills like listening, visiting and mentoring, often unpaid and performed by women, are valued.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It also reinforces interdependence: helping a neighbour today means someone will help you tomorrow.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As I shared in my Budget speech, Ain, a mother, volunteers in our community.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One hour of her time visiting a hospitalised neighbour is as valuable as one hour of a lawyer volunteering at a legal clinic.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Could this be hosted on existing digital infrastructure like Giving.sg?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If not, is the Government exploring alternative ways to strengthen neighbourliness and mutual aid?

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, in the age of AI, the arts and culture will be more important than ever.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: I am very glad that the SG Culture Pass, an idea raised by former Nominated Member of Parliament Terence Ho, has been launched.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: I hope that the arts will be seen as a staple of life in Singapore, alongside sports.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: The Culture Pass covers a range of activities spanning heritage, visual arts, theatre, music, dance, film and now, Singapore literature.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: It would be wonderful if the Culture Pass could encourage Singaporeans to try something different from what they are accustomed to.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: For example, could it persuade a heritage buff to step into the theatre for the first time?

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Assuming there will be regular top-ups of the Culture Pass, I would like to suggest offering first-timer discounts or bonus credits when a person spends Culture Pass credits in a new category that he or she has not previously used the credits for.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: A discount arrangement could be worked out with participating arts and heritage organisations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Age-related proficiency loss also occurred in other countries but was particularly pronounced in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: This is a concern as literacy reflects the ability to handle and process new information.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: I remember the days when bookstores could be found all across Singapore – from second-hand bookstores in Far East Plaza to the MPH flagship store along Stamford Road.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: While the book publishing and distribution business model has changed with the times, and we cannot expect a similar density of bookstores as in the past, there is still something special about bookstores that is worth preserving.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: They are places to discover new authors, often serendipitously, browse the latest titles, and access the ideas that are trending across the world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: In this sense, bookstores could be considered a public good that encourages reading and contributes to the publishing ecosystem, complementing our public libraries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Terence Ho (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps commercial developers could even be granted additional gross floor area if they lease premises to bookstores that fulfil certain community objectives.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: By the numbers, our arts ecosystem appears supported and healthy.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The public sector outcomes review reports rising heritage awareness, stable graduate employment in the arts, and growing attendance at festivals and community programmes.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And if, our arts ecosystem is so well supported, why does it remain so fragile?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Substation had already closed its doors back in 2021.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Last month, Pangdemonium announced its final season after 16 years.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Each closure had its own reasons, but when established companies with a track record and loyal audiences cannot sustain themselves or choose to stop as the conditions have become too demanding, then it is not just a series of individual decisions.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Yet, donation to the arts make up less than 2% of total charitable giving in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On the demand side, there is a paradox.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This same survey also points us towards answers.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It found that Singaporeans with childhood exposure to the arts were significantly more likely to value, attend and advocate for the arts as adults.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Students and youths already have among the highest physical attendance rates for performances.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The data tell us both where the gap is and where the opportunity lies.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First, introduce micro grants for small scale community-facing arts projects.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They should come with simplified administration criteria and should not be packed to a percentage of an overall budget.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For small projects, such micro grants could be the difference between a project happening or it not happening at all.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Second, make the arts more affordable and accessible for our youths.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Let us meet their enthusiasm with sustained, expand, expanded and subsidised access.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This could mean expanded subsidised student pricing, extending the SG Culture Pass to students aged 13 to 18, or even exploring co-payments for tickets using funds from their Edusave account.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If we believe that the arts build character, empathy and understanding, then we should treat access to them with the same seriousness we treat access to education and enrichment.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee
text: They work project to project, commission to commission.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee
text: While that gives them independence, it also means they are often disadvantaged when it comes to negotiating fees, contracts, or usage rights.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee
text: Too often, they end up being price takers rather than price makers and take the short stick.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee
text: MCCY has done a lot over the years to support our arts practitioners in funding, talent development, outreach and capability building.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee
text: That has helped grow the sector and strengthen our arts ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee
text: But there is one area that seems to have been left a little behind: legal support.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee
text: When you are self-employed, understanding contracts, intellectual property rights, and negotiating commercial terms is not just useful, but essential.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee
text: However, without guidance and support, talented artists can find themselves underselling their work or signing away rights they should not.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee
text: Many are particularly disadvantaged when dealing with large commercial organisations.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee
text: Professional help exists but, as I have noted in this House before, lawyers can be expensive.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee
text: This affects not just their earnings, but also the sustainability of their careers in the arts.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee
text: So, I want to ask, would MCCY consider looking at ways to help self-employed arts practitioners navigate the legal aspects of commercialising their art?

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee
text: This could be through legal literacy programmes, templates for contracts, or access to affordable legal advisory services.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee
text: Assisting them with commercial or legal negotiations would also be of great help for our arts practitioners.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee
text: Supporting them in this way frees them up to concentrate on their art and strengthen their careers.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee
text: At the end of the day, talent alone is not enough.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee
text: Artists need to be empowered to protect their work and negotiate on their own terms so that our arts ecosystem can continue to thrive.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim
text: Chairman, I declare interest as the chief executive officer of EtonHouse Community Fund (ECF), an IPC charity focused on nurturing the potential of children and youths, as well as Director on the Board of Singapore Business Federation Foundation.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim
text: I will touch on: nurturing confident youths, active citizenry and ground-up initiatives, as well as making businesses do better.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim
text: It is unenviable how young Singaporeans today live lives.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim
text: There is more of everything and yet many feel and wonder if there are ever enough.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim
text: Singapore's young must believe they have a place and a future here in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim
text: I look forward to an update on the SG Youth Action Plan, especially intentional efforts to nurture confidence.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim
text: I hope MCCY expands partnerships on these efforts and collaborate with partners, particularly for mentoring and work-experience efforts, so that youths get access to mentors, internships and real-world opportunities.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim
text: In East Coast Group Representation Constituency (GRC), we have the youth internship programme; and I think some of the students are joining us here in the House today.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim
text: When young people can see the path towards meaningful roles and future opportunities, it builds confidence and hope.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim
text: Our young have some of the biggest hearts.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim
text: When I was lecturing at Temasek Polytechnic over a decade ago, I led several local and international service trips.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim
text: My students were more than arms and legs.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim
text: I look forward to more details, including priority areas and support offered for Singaporeans who are keen to apply.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim
text: Being in the impact space for close to 15 years, Chairman, I see first-hand how many charities and community organisations are doing important work and how more help is often needed.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim
text: This is helpful as the enhanced fundraising programme is tapering to pre-pandemic levels and several charity friends have shared their concerns with me.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim
text: Chairman, in conclusion, let us draw inspiration from our young, their big hearts and strong sense of social justice.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim
text: There is one Malay saying that goes, "Pemuda harapan bangsa, pemudi tiang negara", which means the youths are the hope of the nation and pillars of society.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim
text: And that belief, Chairman, is what will carry us to the future.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, I would like to declare my interest as my union operates a credit co-operative and I am a member of the Singapore National Co-operative Executive Council.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Co-operatives are formed because Singaporeans believe strongly in the principles of self-help and mutual assistance.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: This spirit of fellowship brings them together to provide services that uplift their members and support communities at large.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: During Singapore's formative years, the co-operative movement attracted individuals who drove initiatives that include consumer co-operatives which provide affordable essentials, and thrift and loan co-operatives that offer accessible financial services.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Consequently, they became key pillars in providing affordable, quality and accessible goods and services to workers and vulnerable communities.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: These demonstrated their continued commitment to invest alongside public support in serving communities.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: With rising competition from more private entities, including global brand names, co-operatives in Singapore are experiencing challenges in attracting youth involvement, talent attraction and retention to continue their mission.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Separately, there is also the broader question of how to encourage the formation of new co-operatives to meet emerging community needs.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: As we look ahead, can the Ministry share, how will it support co-operatives in community engagement, youth involvement and ease of formation of new co-operatives so that more Singaporeans can adopt the co-operative model to address community needs?

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: What will be done to encourage co-operatives to scale up and remain sustainable?

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Can the Ministry consider reviewing aspects of the Co-operative Societies Act to allow for greater flexibility in their operations, including allowing enterprises to form co-operatives, different from the current rule whereby only individuals and unions can form co-operatives?

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Further, can the Ministry support co-operatives by reviewing the current Central Co-operative Fund contribution rate to ensure it is comparable with the current corporate tax rate?

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: That way, co-operatives can channel the savings to support more members and the community.

speaker: Mr Sanjeev Kumar Tiwari (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, in a world of rapid change, cooperatives are built on trust, powered by likeminded people, reminding us that success is not measured by profits alone but by how many lives are uplifted and how many futures secured and progress shared.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Chairman, OBS was established in 1967 by Dr Goh Keng Swee to cultivate ruggedness, resilience, leadership and character through outdoor experiential learning.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It formed part of early nation-building efforts to prepare young Singaporeans for life's uncertainties.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: From its beginnings on Pulau Ubin, OBS has grown into a key national institution delivering character and leadership programmes for youths.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In recent years, OBS has expanded its reach and upgraded its facilities.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Under the National Outdoor Adventure Education Masterplan, a new OBS@Coney campus was developed and when fully operational, it is expected to significantly increase OBS' annual capacity, reinforcing the Government's commitment to outdoor education as part of holistic development.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Today, the OBS experience is most closely associated with youths for many young people.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is a formative rite of passage that fosters resilience and social cohesion.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: By building on existing partnerships, could OBS collaborate with grassroots networks, for example, to design adapted programmes for even older adults and community groups?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With appropriate adjustments, I believe that OBS' ethos of resilience and teamwork can be translated into accessible inter-generational experiences that foster connections across age, ethnic and social groups.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Such partnerships could help bridge generational divides, encouraging lifelong learning and creating shared experiences that deepen community bonds.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Exploring these possibilities would broaden OBS' role beyond youth development, strengthening our social fabric and reinforcing a shared Singaporean identity.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen
text: In Ireland, Jigsaw operates youth mental health cafes – low-stigma drop-in spaces that have significantly reduced barriers to help-seeking.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen
text: In Australia, Headspace combines informal hangout areas with on-site mental health, work and study support.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen
text: These models work because they meet young people where they are, without requiring them to formally seek help.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen
text: In Singapore, traditional spaces like void decks have "No Football" signs put up and malls require spending, which may discourage youths from utilising them as third spaces.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen
text: We need intermediate spaces in our heartlands, not clinical settings, but places where young people can play, socialise and access support early before conditions escalate.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen
text: Will the Government pilot third space hubs in our heartlands, co-locating informal hangout areas with access to mental health, mentoring and work-study support?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen
text: Will MCCY develop a national plan to repurpose void decks and community spaces into free, youth-friendly spaces that facilitate social connection?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan
text: But in Singapore, this is a serious and growing challenge that interacts with something very specific to us – our relationship with space.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan
text: Singapore is a land-scare country where every square metre must justify its economic value.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan
text: We have parks, Community Centres and integrated hubs, like One Tampines Hub.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan
text: There is a difference between programmed spaces and unstructured open spaces.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan
text: Many of our communal facilities are curated with specific demographics and aims in mind.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan
text: They function well as spaces of organised activity but less well as spaces of spontaneous encounter.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan
text: It was the default third space for an entire generation of Singaporeans, including mine.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan
text: There, community happened without anyone having to organise or pay for it.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan
text: But the ground-level openness that made the void deck a place you passed through and stayed in has given way to something more structured, purposeful and less porous.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan
text: I invite the House to consider what is the default third space for young Singaporeans today.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan
text: Where can they show up without a booking, a programme or a minimum spend?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan
text: And have the kind of organic encounters that build friendships, spark passion projects and forge civic bonds?

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan
text: Young Singaporeans are already trying to answer this themselves.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan
text: We see it in ground-up initiatives, like FriendZone and the Casual Poet Library.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan
text: These are signs of unmet need for spaces that are free and open to all, where people can just be.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan
text: Mr Chairman, we cannot build a "we first" society through youth panels and volunteerism drives alone.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan
text: Spaces that treat the need to gather and belong, not as a luxury, but as essential social infrastructure.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, I welcome the Ministry's continued investments in youth engagement platforms, traineeships and pathways into employment.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: Coupled with the strong academic attainment of our youths as evidenced in our performance on international benchmarks, these initiatives will undoubtedly help prepare our young people for economic participation amid the demands of an increasingly competitive global environment.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: This is particularly important in a digital age where their values, aspirations and sense of belonging are shaped by global influences.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: National surveys, such as the Health Promotion Board's Students' Health Survey and the National Youth Council's National Youth Survey, have highlighted concerns related to stress, mental well-being and life pressures among young people.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: Complementing these findings, national mental health studies indicate that a significant proportion of youth report symptoms of anxiety, depression or psychological distress.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: Studies, such as the 2020 UNICEF Digital Lives of Children in ASEAN and the Infocomm Media Development Authority's Digital Society Survey, highlight that young people today are highly connected digitally and increasingly exposed to a wide range of information, perspectives and social influences through online environments.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: More than a century ago, sociologist Émile Durkheim observed that when the social groups individuals belong to weaken, people become increasingly reliant on themselves alone.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: His insight remains relevant today, as young people navigate identity formation in a rapidly changing social and digital environment.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: We understand from research that adolescents who report a stronger sense of belonging to their national or community context may demonstrate higher levels of well-being, social trust and resilience during key life transitions.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: Conversely, where opportunities for participation in shared institutions or community life are limited, young people may report greater uncertainty in identity formation, which may, in turn, be associated with lower perceived well-being.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: Opportunities to participate in civic or community settings then may serve not only social purposes but also contribute to psychosocial outcomes that support long-term well-being.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: Identity formation does not arise solely from instruction or programme participation, but through opportunities for shared responsibility, meaningful participation and voice.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: One of them pertain to the extent to which our citizens have a meaningful voice in shaping how they are supported.

speaker: Prof Kenneth Poon (Nominated Member)
text: I look forward to the Minister's response on this matter.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Many say they feel more anxious speaking face-to-face than online.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: If a young person repeatedly feels unseen or peripheral, that experience becomes part of how they see themselves and their place in society.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: So, the question before us is not only how to run more programmes.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: It is this: are we designing everyday Singapore in a way that makes connection easy or effortful?

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: I suggest we focus on two levers: spaces and programming.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: A young man once told me that when he felt overwhelmed, he would go to the skate park in Tampines.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: He did not go there for a structured activity.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: He went because it was where he felt understood.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: That linkway had quietly become a rehearsal space, a place where they practised, formed friendships and improved together.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: The provision of mirrored space at Marina South Pier MRT acknowledged that informal spaces matter.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Youths tell me that they compete for library seats or spend money at cafes just to have somewhere to study together.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Community Clubs exist, but booking systems can feel formal, adult-controlled or difficult for spontaneous use.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: If our spaces feel distant or procedural, young people simply retreat to their rooms and to their screens.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: She books a small multi-use room in her neighbourhood Community Club with two taps on an app.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: It is available because certain off-peak hours are designated youth-access blocks.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: She and her friends rehearse a dance routine.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Next door, a group of students are revising together.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: An uncle from the neighbourhood drops by to conduct a small mentoring session, matched through a community platform.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Incorporate small acoustically treated multi-use rooms in future precinct upgrades.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: It is about existing infrastructure being more youth intentional.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: A secondary school student recently wrote to me, asking if she could put posters to match volunteer music teachers with learners who lacked access.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Her instinct was right: connection happens when people teach, learn and serve together.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: But why should she have to rely on void deck posters?

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Imagine instead: a neighbourhood-based matching feature within existing community apps.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: A polytechnic student who plays the violin indicates she can volunteer for two hours a week.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: A Primary 5 student who cannot afford lessons signs up.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: The match is facilitated through the Community Club.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: And when generations interact regularly, identity becomes shared, not fragmented.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: I also hope that MCCY can consider how we can nurture cross-generational mangling as well.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Chairman, if loneliness is rising, the response is not only more services.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: It is better design, design spaces that are easy to access, design systems that match initiative with opportunity, design programmes that reward continuity.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: From a youth's perspective, the difference is simple.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Instead of asking, "Where can I go?", the answer becomes obvious: "Right here." That is what it means to design belonging, not as a slogan, but as everyday reality.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Chairman, in a "we first" society, our youth are not just beneficiaries of Singapore's future.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: They must also be partners in shaping it.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Over the past year, MCCY has engaged many young Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: But the key question is how these conversations translate into sustained pathways for participation.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Young Singaporeans today grow up in a very different environment.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: They face economic uncertainties, rapid technological change and the constant pressures of the digital world.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Member Dr Charlene Chen just spoke about loneliness in our interconnected world today.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Therefore, how is MCCY equipping our young people with the resilience to navigate these pressures while remaining grounded in a sense of shared responsibility for Singapore?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: What opportunities are there for young Singaporeans to step forward meaningfully in community building, policymaking and service to society?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: For example, how can our youths be more actively involved in shaping local initiatives, volunteering networks or national conversations?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Ultimately, the goal is not simply to encourage participation, but to cultivate partnership but to nurture a generation that sees Singapore not just a place to live but as a community they feel responsible for, because when they feel a genuine stake in Singapore, they and we collectively, can unlock the fecundity of their ideas, the initiative and civic imagination.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: I would appreciate therefore the Minister's thoughts on how we can continue building such a generation.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: Mr Chairman, I thank Members for their speeches and suggestions and their strong support for the work that we do at MCCY.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: For 60 years, we lived out our ideals of becoming "one united people, regardless of race, language or religion." In writing the Singapore pledge in 1966, our founding father, Mr S Rajaratnam, articulated his vision of building an inclusive "Singaporean" identity anchored in our model of multiculturalism.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: Fresh off the uncertainty of separation, we chose to build a united, shared and equal existence as a "we first" collective, rather than co-existence as divided, isolated and competing "me first" communities.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: Over 60 years, we have built a cohesive multicultural community, where we identify with one another as Singaporeans first.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: While Singapore is often noted for our exceptional Third World to First World economic story, what is equally, if not more, exceptional, is our success in fostering a cohesive multicultural society amidst great diversity in race, language and religion.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
text: Today, we again face the uncertainty of a changed world.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Mr David Neo)
